articles.title: Building an AI Shirt Agent with Spring AI and Tool Calling
articles.excerpt: Why a Shirt Recommender Is a Good First Spring AI Project Most tutorials that introduce large language models to Java developers start with a chatbot that answers questions. That is a useful starting…
articles.body: Why a Shirt Recommender Is a Good First Spring AI Project Most tutorials that introduce large language models to Java developers start with a chatbot that answers questions. That is a useful starting point, but it hides the part that makes LLM features valuable inside a real application: the model has to take an action that your code controls. A chatbot that only produces text is a demo. An agent that looks something up in your own system and returns a structured result is a feature. This article walks through shirts-agent , a small Spring Boot and Spring AI example that makes the idea concrete. A user sends an item and a color to a REST endpoint. An AI agent calls a Java method that searches an in-memory catalog, and the service returns a structured shirt recommendation.

articles.title: Live Poll State for Late Joiners: Snapshot and Diff Without Trusting Clients
articles.excerpt: Short answer: keep one server-owned poll snapshot, attach a monotonically increasing revision, and send later changes as diffs. A client that joins late asks for the current snapshot first, then appli…
articles.body: Short answer: keep one server-owned poll snapshot, attach a monotonically increasing revision, and send later changes as diffs. A client that joins late asks for the current snapshot first, then applies diffs only when the revision is exactly the next one. This keeps a marketplace session's vote totals coherent and limits what an untrusted browser can assert. The data flow is deliberately plain. A poll service owns the canonical question, options, counts, and revision. A connection receives a snapshot, then subscribes to an ordered stream of patches. The browser renders the snapshot immediately; it does not reconstruct history from local events. If a gap appears, it requests another snapshot.

articles.title: Certificate enrollment hygiene after CVE-2026-84790
articles.excerpt: Certificate enrollment hygiene after CVE-2026-84790 The fix for CVE-2026-84790 ships in OpenVPN 2.7.8. The condition that made the flaw useful sits earlier in the chain, at the point where an authorit…
articles.body: Certificate enrollment hygiene after CVE-2026-84790 The fix for CVE-2026-84790 ships in OpenVPN 2.7.8. The condition that made the flaw useful sits earlier in the chain, at the point where an authority signs a certificate whose subject field contains a null byte. What the authority should reject Subject fields carry attributes such as common name, organizational unit and email address. Standards describe how to encode them, and a policy can state which characters are acceptable. A simple rule covers the flaw's shape: reject any attribute containing a non-printing character, including NUL, and reject attributes whose encoded length disagrees with the decoded string. The rule applies to common names most of all, because that is the attribute most tools read as identity.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady . What I Built CSV files are everywhere. Unfortunately, so are the little inconsistencies that make them frustrating to work with: extra whitespace, currency symbols, inconsistent date formats, missing-value placeholders, and duplicate records. Cleaning those problems manually is tedious. Automating the process blindly can be worse. CSV Rescue is a local-first, open-source application that uses AI to identify useful cleaning operations, lets the user approve them, and then applies the selected changes through predictable Python code. The idea is simple: let AI figure out what might need fixing, but don't let it invent the fixes. The workflow has three steps: Upload a CSV file for local analysis.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: 1, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.

articles.body: Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, " Lost on Paradise ", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week. Foster famously ghost-wrote the first " Star Wars " novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit.
